title: Platner Drops His Senate Bid, and Who Should Replace Him
body:
It is official. Graham Platner has dropped his bid for U.S. Senate after his former partner, Jenny Racicot, accused him of rape, an allegation I find credible and abhorrent. He denies it. His exit comes just before the deadline that lets the Maine Democratic Party select his replacement to take on Susan Collins.

A personal note: I volunteered on Platner's campaign from the beginning, but this accusation forced me to leave immediately. I have a zero-tolerance policy for behavior of this kind, and I support his decision to drop out.

So where does that leave Maine? Thousands of people were energized by a populist, anti-billionaire, working-class message. They are now betrayed and disappointed, with nowhere to put that energy and no candidate in a race against a senator who has repeatedly outrun her polls and outlasted scandal.

Platner beat Janet Mills in a landslide because Maine made a clear choice: not an establishment Democrat, but a progressive outsider. The replacement who best matches that is former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, a working-class progressive from a family of northern Maine loggers, with the experience Platner lacked and real name recognition. Bellows or Wood could carry the energy too, but Jackson strikes me as the most logical pick to harness it.

I break down the full field over on Food and Politics.

title: Susan Collins Faces Scrutiny Over ICE Shooting in Maine
body:
Senator Collins is under scrutiny this week after ICE agents shot and killed Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero in Biddeford. Reporting indicates he was legally authorized to work in the US and was not the initial target of the surveillance operation. He was a well-known member of his community, survived by his wife and young daughter.

The shooting, the second ICE-related killing this week, sparked large protests at the Scarborough detention center, with ire directed at both ICE and Collins. She has spent months touting her efforts to scale back ICE activity in Maine, but that sits uneasily beside her vote to fund the agency after Democrats shut it down from February to April demanding policy changes. Her office is now calling for an end to non-essential ICE activity in the state, and the administration says it is halting vehicle stops.

For the Senate race, the lesson of the week is that the energy Graham Platner harnessed is still very much present in Maine, even if the movement is currently without a head. These protests will factor into the Democratic Party's choice of his successor later this month, and could hurt Collins in future polling once a nominee is selected to face her.

title: Dan Osborn, Nebraska's Independent Candidate
body:
Over in Nebraska, an independent with no major-party ties keeps making waves in this November's Senate race. Dan Osborn is a union leader, industrial mechanic, and Navy veteran who rose to prominence leading the 2021 Kellogg's strike in Omaha, was fired shortly after (he says in retaliation), and ran as an independent against Senator Deb Fischer in 2024. In deep-red Nebraska he polled shockingly close, some surveys even had it tied, before Fischer held on. Now he is back, running against the state's other Republican incumbent, Pete Ricketts.

Osborn's campaign is meaningful for the same reason Platner's was in Maine: both turned working-class disillusionment into a statewide movement against a powerful incumbent. I want to be clear that I am comparing the movements, not the men or their character. There is also an unconfirmed accusation floating around that Osborn recruited Platner to run in Maine, a piece of drama still playing out that I will keep watching. What the two share is a populist, anti-billionaire, pro-worker message that lands in places the political establishment left behind.

Nebraska is one of those places. Its economy leans heavily on agriculture, an industry gutted over decades by consolidation as large conglomerates buy up small farms and control prices, and now squeezed further by Trump-era tariffs cutting the value of exported goods. That financial pressure has bred a deep frustration, and Osborn has managed to harness it.

On The Needle Project, I built this race factoring in Nebraska's strong Republican lean and Osborn's 2024 performance, and right now Ricketts holds the edge. But that does not yet factor in polling, because the only substantial polls so far were funded by the Osborn camp and have been questioned on methodology. Quality nonpartisan polling is still missing. The Democratic nominee, Cindy Burbank, has dropped out to back Osborn. My read: Osborn has tapped into something real in rural America, anti-billionaire and pro-worker candidates have done well in 2026, and once quality polls land I expect them to show a tighter race than the fundamentals suggest, close all the way to November.

title: Jackson Holds the Delegate Advantage Ahead of the July 23 Debate
body:
A quick note on the Maine Senate replacement race: a vast majority of the chosen Democratic delegates who will select Maine's replacement nominee were supportive of Troy Jackson's bid, giving him a heavy advantage heading into the upcoming debate between the major candidates on July 23 on CNN.

The party must certify its new nominee by July 27, so the debate is effectively the field's last big chance to move delegates before the vote. Once the nominee is set, the Maine Senate needle comes back online with the new matchup.

title: A Nominee? Before Nomination Day?
body:
Yes and no. Technically, Troy Jackson hasn't officially been picked as the party nominee, but the title isn't clickbait: he is definitely the presumptive nominee, and something strange would need to happen for that to change in five days.

Here is the process. After Graham Platner dropped his bid, the Maine Democratic Party had each county's Democrats meet to elect delegates, who will attend a convention on July 25 and vote on the next nominee for Senate. They have not voted yet, but we already have plenty of clues about who they will pick, which is what led the major contenders to drop out. This past weekend, 500 of the 601 delegate slots were selected across the state. Of those 500, more than 460 confirmed they will support Troy Jackson, giving him a commanding portion of the convention before it even meets.

After that, nearly all of the other Democrats dropped out. Nirav Shah ended his campaign Sunday evening and endorsed Jackson, along with Jordan Wood and Dan Kleban. Shenna Bellows also ended her bid, and Paige Loud exited earlier in the weekend. At this point it is a foregone conclusion: Troy Jackson is the new Democratic nominee for Senate, and he will face Susan Collins in November.

Who is he? Born in Fort Kent and raised in Allagash, Jackson served in the Maine State Senate (2008-2014 and 2016-2024), including as Senate president and majority leader, representing northern Aroostook County. His career is a study in evolution: he first ran as a Republican, was first elected as an Independent, and joined the Democratic Party in 2004. Once a social conservative, he shifted to earn 100% scorecards from the Planned Parenthood Action Fund and EqualityMaine. His platform has always centered on health care and workers' rights, and in 2016 he used his superdelegate vote for Bernie Sanders over Hillary Clinton. He has drawn endorsements from Ro Khanna, the Maine DSA, and Hasan Piker.

His platform is pro-worker and anti-billionaire, aimed at making Maine affordable for working people: codifying abortion rights federally, Medicare for All, banning conversion therapy, and stronger anti-discrimination law. He supports aid to Ukraine and opposes an Iran war. He backs fully abolishing and dismantling ICE, has called Israel's campaign in Gaza a genocide, and says he would not support additional military aid to Israel.

What does it mean? Jackson can rise to the movement Platner built before his implosion, riding the same upswell of disillusionment and discontent with billionaires, the Israeli government, and rising costs. He is not the best public speaker in the world, but he offers the same platform with deep experience in the state, a track record of listening to constituents, and a real base among rural, working-class Mainers. He has been at this movement far longer than Platner and is a well-known name. Polling has put Jackson and Collins in a dead heat, and that will be worth watching all the way to November.

title: How James Talarico Could Actually Win in Texas
body:
The Texas Senate race is one of the most interesting matchups of the entire 2026 cycle: Democratic nominee James Talarico against Republican Ken Paxton, set in the largest and most solid Republican stronghold in the country. And yet Talarico has not been trailing in reputable polling. The two have been in a dead heat since they were nominated. Here is why.

First, the setting. Texas is the second-largest state by population and has voted Republican for a very long time. The last Democrat to win a Senate seat here was Lloyd Bentsen in 1988, and the last to carry it in a presidential race was Jimmy Carter in 1976. But there have been close calls, most memorably Beto O'Rourke's 2018 run, which came within about 220,000 votes of unseating Ted Cruz. A perfect storm has now formed that gives Talarico some serious advantages.

The biggest of those advantages is his opponent. Ken Paxton is so entrenched in drama that many Texas Republicans have distanced themselves from him: a 2015 securities-fraud indictment still pending eleven years later, a 2023 impeachment by his own party's House (he was acquitted), whistleblower retaliation that cost the state millions, and an affair that ended his marriage. Nearly a quarter of Republicans who voted in his primary view him unfavorably, which could keep them home in November. He is also endorsed by a president whose popularity is sliding.

Talarico brings his own strengths. He is a devout Christian and an aspiring Presbyterian minister with a theology degree, which makes him very hard to corner on scripture in a religious, conservative state, and he uses that fluency to push back on GOP talking points. He is also an 8th-generation Texan, his family here for over 200 years, which carries weight in a state with deep state-centric pride. And Texas' large Latino population, which swung toward Trump in 2024, has shown signs of regret after ICE operations, with some evidence of rising Latino turnout and a shift back toward Democrats.

What does it all mean? A deeply unpopular Paxton and a genuinely popular Talarico have combined into a set of factors that keep this race tied, which is rare for a state this conservative. The race still leans Republican, and the needle reflects that, but Talarico has a real chance at an upset. He is the underdog story of this cycle, and absolutely worth watching.

title: El-Sayed Defeats Stevens. Will the Dems Adapt?
body:
Abdul El-Sayed has defeated Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, NBC News projects, winning by about 2 points. This is the open seat Gary Peters is vacating, Mike Rogers is unopposed on the GOP side, and it is a must-hold for any Democratic path to the majority. His victory is also highly symbolic for the future of the Democratic party.

Michigan is one of the last true purple states, flipping between the parties in consecutive cycles: Trump in 2024 (while simultaneously sending Democrat Elissa Slotkin to the Senate), Biden in 2020, Trump in 2016, Obama in 2012. So how Michigan voters approached this primary may be a glimpse of how the party approaches future elections here. This began as a three-way race between Mallory McMorrow, El-Sayed, and Stevens. McMorrow suspended her campaign in July, though her name stayed on the ballot, and her exit consolidated establishment backing behind Stevens.

El-Sayed is an epidemiologist, the former Detroit Health Director, and a former Wayne County health department head who lost a gubernatorial primary to Gretchen Whitmer. He ran on Medicare for All, getting money out of politics, anti-billionaire rhetoric, and sharp criticism of Israel. He has explicitly said he is not a Democratic Socialist, but a large share of his base identifies that way, and so do his endorsements. Stevens, a congresswoman since 2019, ran a far more moderate campaign on manufacturing, tariffs, auto jobs, and affordability, but it ended up defined more by her AIPAC backing and establishment support. The race drew over $41 million in outside spending, more than half of it pro-Stevens or anti-El-Sayed.

El-Sayed represents a movement brewing since Bernie Sanders' 2016 campaign, the one that produced Ocasio-Cortez, Cori Bush, Pressley, Tlaib, and Omar. It stalled after the 2024 red shift and has surged back this cycle through candidates like Graham Platner (now Troy Jackson), El-Sayed, Zohran Mamdani, Donovan McKinney, and Janeese Lewis George. But the same night complicates the story: Cori Bush lost again in Missouri, another grassroots Democrat falling to an incumbent with establishment support. The left is winning open seats and struggling against incumbents.

Still, a win in a purple state sends a clear message. Michigan was offered a centrist establishment Democrat and a progressive populist outsider whose views diverge sharply from Democratic leadership, and Michigan chose Abdul. The real question is whether the party adapts. This wave amounts to a slowly building vote of no confidence in Schumer-era strategy, and the party is notorious for being disconnected from its own base. Will the DSCC, Schumer, and Whitmer consolidate behind El-Sayed, or stay quiet as Schumer did with Troy Jackson in Maine?

I will not ignore the tension still in this race. The coalition that won the primary is not the obvious favorite in November. The final EPIC-MRA poll in late July had Stevens beating Rogers 44-42 while Rogers led El-Sayed 46-43, both inside a four-point margin. Data for Progress in late June put El-Sayed ahead of Rogers 47-46, though that poll was commissioned by the Working Families Party. Weigh it how you like, but neither side is running away with this. Rogers is Trump-backed, unopposed, and sitting in a race still rated a toss-up after losing to Slotkin by 19,000 votes on a night Trump carried the state. Whether Michigan Democrats close ranks or relitigate the primary for three months will tell us more about this party than the primary itself did.

title: Turek Slips in Iowa, Talarico Holds Lead in Texas
body:
New polls in the Iowa and Texas Senate races have moved the needles in the model.

Iowa: Emerson, a quality nonpartisan pollster, has Democrat Josh Turek trailing Republican Ashley Hinson 45-48. Since we started tracking this race, Turek led by about a point on average, so this shifts the needle measurably in Hinson's favor. Some fascinating internals: Turek is actually winning independents 49 to 38, but his approval in the state sits at 27% against Hinson's 40%. Iowa leans right, and Turek now faces an uphill battle to close the gap after enjoying a lead in earlier polls. He is struggling to outpace Hinson's attacks, which have centered on his absence from 60% of votes in the Iowa House and perceived outside influence from PACs.

Texas: a new Texas Southern University Barbara Jordan Center poll puts James Talarico ahead of Ken Paxton 47 to 45. The Barbara Jordan Center is highly ranked for its methodology, and this solidifies a lead Talarico first started building in a Fox News poll at the end of July.

Paxton has continued to fail at consolidating his own party, with only 85% of Republicans pledging support while Talarico holds 97% of Democrats. Talarico is also overperforming with independents and Republicans: 5% of GOP voters say they will flip and vote for him, and he takes 63% of independents to Paxton's 23%. He also leads among women, Black voters, and Hispanic voters, while Paxton leads by 14 among white voters, a group Trump won by 33 in 2024. All of this is juxtaposed with Republicans leading almost every other major race polled in Texas. The poll shows Paxton's continued struggle to establish himself as a quality alternative, and Talarico's continued success building a broad coalition in a state that dominantly supports Republicans. There is major potential here for a Talarico-led upset.

The needle shifts: in Iowa, Hinson gains ground and now holds a 73% chance of victory. In Texas, the needle stays largely the same, with a slight shift in Talarico's direction.

Keep in mind that both of these needles give a slight bonus to the Republican candidate, because both states lean right. Even when the Democrat leads in polls, the Republican can still hold the higher likelihood of victory, as is the case in both races here.

title: Markey vs Moulton: Is It Really a Dead Heat?
body:
A quick look at a race outside our tracker. Seth Moulton, hoping to unseat longtime incumbent Ed Markey in the Massachusetts Democratic Senate primary, has ramped up his ad campaign, and after recent polling his team put out a release calling the race a statistical dead heat. The two candidates are not vastly different, but let me break it down.

Markey is an 80-year-old incumbent with more than 53 years in elected office, in the Senate since a 2013 special election. His age matters here only because it is a central argument of the Moulton campaign. On policy, Markey co-sponsors Medicare for All and single-payer universal health care, authored and champions the Green New Deal, and is an active supporter of LGBTQ rights and structural progressive change. Despite his age, he is likely the more liberal candidate in this race.

Moulton is no upstart either. A 47-year-old Marine Corps veteran, he has represented Massachusetts' 6th district since 2014 and briefly ran for president in 2020. He supports expanding Medicare access but wants to keep a private option rather than single-payer, backs climate action but emphasizes bipartisan solutions over the Green New Deal, and has had a complicated history with the LGBTQ community despite insisting he is fully supportive. He runs on generational change, pragmatism, and bipartisanship, and is the slightly more moderate of the two.

Early polling gave Markey a dominant lead, but it has tightened: UNH had him up 46-33 in April, Emerson 37-32 in May, and UNH 41-35 in late June. After that last poll the Moulton camp declared a statistical dead heat. That is not quite a factual statement, though the sentiment that the race is narrowing is certainly true.

Here is the breakdown. Markey holds a double-digit lead among registered Democrats, which is his strong suit and a throughline across every poll. Moulton leads independents by around 6 points, and turning those independents out is likely his best path in September. The problem for Moulton is that registered Democrats are far more likely to vote in a primary than independents, and Markey has name recognition Moulton does not. So calling this a dead heat is false, and Markey still holds the advantage.

That said, Moulton's aggressive TV campaign started right after the last UNH poll, so Markey could still shed some support in the coming weeks. Polls closer to the September date will likely show further narrowing, and could set up an interesting election day.

title: New Polls and Needle Shifts
body:
A roundup of the latest polling across the Senate races, and where the needles move.

Markey vs. Moulton: A new UMass Amherst poll damaged Seth Moulton's framing of his race against Markey as a dead heat, an idea I wrote about earlier when the polls were tightening. The new number shows Ed Markey up a full 28 points. Moulton still performed well with independents, but Markey dominated the other groups, especially registered Democrats and women. One caveat: primary polling is particularly dicey and far from exact, as we saw in Wisconsin, where Francesca Hong lost on election day despite going in as the polling favorite.

Paxton vs. Talarico: A new Emerson College/Nexstar poll in Texas put Paxton ahead of Talarico by a point, 47-46. Emerson is a relatively strong nonpartisan pollster, and this is the first poll since June 21 to give Paxton any lead. Most public aggregators still lean Talarico, but my model is a little different here. Texas is Republican home territory. Talarico has led on average, has far fewer skeletons, and has outperformed one of the strongest Texas Democrats in recent memory in O'Rourke. But my theory is that the undecided Republicans and conservative independents who have knocked Paxton for his shaky record will still come home, at least a chunk of them, when it is time to vote. Voting for a bad Republican is easier to stomach for some of those voters than voting for any Democrat. My model gives Republicans an advantage in Texas by design, to offer a more pragmatic view and to avoid overestimating the liberal candidate, so I still lean slightly toward Paxton in my forecast.

That is not to say Talarico lacks a route. I have written extensively about his high-quality campaign and his very viable path. It just means organizers need to keep hammering his message home, because this race is a toss-up in every sense. Talarico's supporters should not be discouraged by this poll; this is shaping up to be one of the best Democratic efforts to flip this seat in recent memory, and his voice has resonated across a broad coalition with months to go. For Paxton, the poll is reassuring, but it should still be a wakeup call. There is a mismatch between this candidate and Texas voters, as he is underperforming in a state where he should be dominating.

Peltola vs. Sullivan: In Alaska, an August 5 poll showed Mary Peltola ahead of Dan Sullivan by two, after a June NYT/Siena poll put Sullivan up two. This has become a sneaky contender for an election-night, or really an election-week, showdown, since Alaska famously takes a long time to count. We will not have a winner here on election night. Peltola is a fascinating candidate given her prior success in a state whose politics do not map neatly onto lower-48 party lines. She is Yup'ik, part of a group that makes up about 5% of Alaska's population, while Natives overall are around 14%, a major voting bloc. Her Alaska-first emphasis seems to be resonating there and with other liberal blocs, positioning her as a real challenger in a normally red stronghold.

Brown vs. Husted: A new August 10 Fox News (Beacon/Shaw) poll in Ohio, a high-quality pollster, put Sherrod Brown ahead by 8, 53-45, widening his lead over Husted and bumping his polling average to +5. Brown's strength appears tied to his high approval alongside lower approval for Trump and Husted. Inflation was voters' top concern, and despite Republicans making up the majority of the sample, Brown still holds a large lead. The race shifts in his favor, though it remains a toss-up.

Current polling averages: Maine Jackson +3, North Carolina Cooper +9, Ohio Brown +5, Texas Talarico +2, Iowa Hinson +1, Georgia Ossoff +10, Nebraska no nonpartisan polling available, Michigan Rogers +4, Alaska Peltola +1.
